text: AWS Budgets lets you set a spending or usage threshold and get notified when activity crosses it — for the whole account, a linked account, or spend filtered down to a specific service or tag. The detail that trips people up: a budget doesn't stop anything on its own, ever. Nothing gets throttled and no resource gets shut down. It's a watchdog, not a brake, and that distinction matters once real money is on the line.

A budget definition is just a scope, a type, an amount, and a period, underneath whatever console workflow sets it up. This one is a COST budget: $800 a month against the whole account. Nothing more complex than that is required to get a working budget running — the alert thresholds that actually notify anyone layer on top of this simple core definition.

A cost budget tracks dollars against a target — alert me if this month is on pace to pass $800. A usage budget tracks a quantity instead, like EC2 instance-hours, which matters when the goal is catching runaway usage before it even turns into a large bill at all. AWS Budgets also covers Reserved Instance and Savings Plans utilization and coverage budgets, which Lesson 28 picks back up from the discount side of the equation.

Each alert threshold can trigger on actual spend, meaning what's already been billed for real, or on forecasted spend, meaning what the current pace projects the full period will reach by the time it closes. A forecasted threshold is the earlier warning of the two — it can fire within the first two weeks of the month, well before actual spend has crossed anything at all. Eighty and a hundred percent are the common threshold pair to set.

An $800 monthly budget with an 80% actual-spend threshold and a separate 100% forecasted threshold catches both a bad pace early and a hard overage as it actually happens — an email goes out to the configured recipients either way, with real time left to act before the invoice closes. Next, Lesson 27 covers finding the waste a budget alert can only ever report after the fact, never prevent on its own.
